According to the Book of Revelation, this is the prophesied gathering place of armies for a final battle during the end times, now used generically for any doomsday scenario — what is it called?
Armageddon (Ancient; Late; from) is the prophesied gathering of armies for a battle during the end times, according to the Book of Revelation in the New Testament of the Christian Bible.

Boris Yeltsin (1 February 1931 - 23 April 2007) was a Soviet and Russian politician who served as President of Russia from 1991 to 1999.

In Greek mythology, this ferryman transported the souls of the properly buried dead across the river bordering the underworld, and demanded a coin placed in the mouth of each corpse as payment — who is he?
Charon (-n; Ancient) is the ferryman of the Greek underworld.

Daedalus was a skillful architect and craftsman, seen as a symbol of wisdom, knowledge and power.

Donald Tusk (born 22 April 1957) is a Polish politician and historian who has served as the prime minister of Poland since 2023, previously holding the office from 2007 to 2014.
This American murderer served as a hitman for his uncle's crime ring during a string of Osage Nation killings, and was ultimately pardoned by Oklahoma's governor in 1966. Who is he?

François-René de Chateaubriand (4 September 1768 - 4 July 1848) was a French writer, politician, diplomat and historian who influenced French literature of the 19th century.

Irene Montero (Spanish; born 13 February 1988) is a Spanish politician, member of the Podemos party.

Jaw Shaw-kong (pinyin: Zho Shokng; born 6 May 1950) is a Taiwanese politician, media personality and entrepreneur.
As military governor of Paris in 1914, this French officer helped win the First Battle of the Marne — famously rushing troops to the front in commandeered taxicabs. Who was he?

Joseph Gallieni (24 April 1849 - 27 May 1916) was a French military officer, active for most of his career as a military commander and administrator in the French colonies where he wrote several books on colonial affairs.
From 2010 to 2023 this Turkish politician ran the Republican People's Party while serving as the country's Leader of the Main Opposition — who is he?
Kemal Kılıçdaroğlu (Turkish; born 17 December 1948), also referred to by his initials KK, is a Turkish politician who served as the leader of the Republican People's Party (CHP) from 2010 to 2023.
Born in Ust-Kamenogorsk, this Imperial Russian general's failed 1917 coup against Kerensky's government ironically boosted the Bolsheviks, before he led White forces in the Civil War — who was he?
Lavr Kornilov was Imperial Russian Army general (1870–1918).
Born in British Hong Kong and trained as a lawyer in the United States, this politician was mayor of Taipei before serving as president of the Republic of China from 2008 to 2016 — who is he?
Ma Ying-jeou (pinyin: M Yngji; Ma-; born 13 July 1950) is a Taiwanese politician, lawyer, and legal scholar who served as the sixth president of the Republic of China from 2008 to 2016.
Queen of England from 1553 and briefly Queen of Spain as the wife of Philip II, she pursued the Marian persecutions that scorched her reputation in history — who was she?
Mary I (18 February 1516 - 17 November 1558) was Queen of England and Ireland from July 1553 and Queen of Spain as the wife of King Philip II from January 1556 until her death in 1558.
Twice shot in the head and surviving both times, this Russian field marshal later defeated Napoleon's invasion using a strategy of attrition — who was he?
Mikhail Kutuzov was Field Marshal of the Russian Empire (1745–1813).
Known in the Austrian court as Franz, Duke of Reichstadt, and to history as 'L'Aiglon,' he reigned as Emperor of the French for just two weeks in 1815 — who was he?
Napoleon II (Napolon Franois Charles Joseph Bonaparte; 20 March 1811 - 22 July 1832) was the disputed Emperor of the French for 2 weeks in 1815.
His conquest of the Liaodong region from the Ming dynasty paved the way for his descendants to found the Qing dynasty in 1636 — who was this founding khan of the Later Jin?
Nurhaci (14 May 1559 - 30 September 1626), also known by his temple name Emperor Taizu of Qing, was the founding khan of the Jurchen-led Later Jin dynasty.

A former commander of the Rwandan Patriotic Front, this politician has been president of Rwanda since 2000, having been the country's de facto leader for years before formally assuming office — who is he?
Paul Kagame (k-; born 23 October 1957) is a Rwandan politician and former military officer who has been the president of Rwanda since 2000, effectively ruling as a dictator.

Married to Frederick, heir apparent to King George II, this woman never became queen consort since her husband died before his father — but she was mother to the future George III and served as presumptive regent until 1756 — who was she?
Princess Augusta of Saxe-Gotha was Princess of Wales, mother of King George III. Augusta's eldest son succeeded her father-in-law as George III in 1760.
Before reaching the White House, this Californian served as Eisenhower's vice president — and would later become the only U.S. president to resign from office. Who was he?
Richard Nixon (January 9, 1913 - April 22, 1994) was the 37th president of the United States, serving from 1969 until his resignation in 1974.
This influential samurai helped overthrow the shogunate during the Meiji Restoration, only to later lead a doomed rebellion against the very government he'd helped create — who was he?
Saigō Takamori (23 January 1828 - 24 September 1877) was a Japanese samurai and politician who was one of the most influential figures in Japanese history.
Born Farid al-Din Khan, this ruler of Bihar and then Bengal went on to defeat the Mughal Empire, seize Delhi, and found his own short-lived empire as its first emperor. Who was he?

Sher Shah Suri (born Farid al-Din Khan; 1472 or 1486 - 22 May 1545), also known by his title Sultan Adil (lit. 'the Just King'), was the Sultan of Hindustan and the first Sur Emperor, ruling from 1540 until his death in 1545.

Located in southern Mesopotamia, in what's now south-central Iraq, this is the earliest known civilization, arising between the 5th and 4th millennium BC along the Tigris and Euphrates rivers - name it?

Vitellius (24 September 15 - 20 December 69) was Roman emperor, ruling for eight months from 19 April to 20 December AD 69.

Wilma Mankiller (November 18, 1945 - April 6, 2010) was a Native American activist, social worker, community developer and the first woman elected to serve as Principal Chief of the Cherokee Nation.

Chaldea: Small Semitic nation of ancient Mesopotamia.

Dzhokhar Dudayev: First President of the Chechen Republic of Ichkeria. From 1962, Dudayev served in the Soviet Air Forces, reaching the rank of major general.

Hezbollah: Islamist movement and militant group based in Lebanon.

Iraqi invasion of Kuwait: Beginning of the 1990–1991 Gulf War.

Psalms: Book of sacred songs in the Hebrew Bible.

Tony Blair: Prime Minister of the United Kingdom from 1997 to 2007.

Patrick Geddes (born 1854) is the earliest of the four.

Henry Vaughan (born 1621) is the earliest of the four. Henry Vaughan (1621 – 23 April 1695) was a Welsh metaphysical poet, author and translator writing in English, and a medical physician.
Which of these four began earliest?
COBOL (founded 1959) is the earliest of the four. COBOL (Common Business-Oriented Language;) is a compiled English-like computer programming language designed for business use.
Which of these four came first?
MATLAB (founded 1984) is the earliest of the four. MATLAB (Matrix Laboratory) is a proprietary multi-paradigm programming language and numeric computing environment developed by MathWorks.
Pick the physicist from these four.
David L. Hill is a physicist.
Who among these is a chemist?
Dmitri Mendeleev is a chemist. The synthetic element mendelevium is named in his honor.
What is the atomic number of Livermorium?
Livermorium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Lv and atomic number 116.
What is the atomic number of Polonium?
Polonium is a chemical element; it has symbol Po and atomic number 84.
In what year did Alan Turing die?
Alan Turing: Alan Mathison Turing (23 June 1912 – 7 June 1954) was an English mathematician, computer scientist, logician, cryptanalyst, philosopher and theoretical biologist.
In what year was Magnesium discovered?
Magnesium is a chemical element; it has symbol Mg and atomic number 12.
Adenosine: Pfizer. Adenosine (symbol A) is an organic compound that occurs widely in nature in the form of diverse derivatives.
In which country is Mikoyan-Gurevich MiG-17 based?
Mikoyan-Gurevich MiG-17: Soviet Union. The MiG-17 was license-built in China as the Shenyang J-5 and Poland as the PZL-Mielec Lim-6.
Who is credited with discovering Niobium?
Niobium: Charles Hatchett. Niobium is a chemical element; it has symbol Nb (formerly columbium, Cb) and atomic number 41.
Who is credited with discovering Peroxisome?
Peroxisome: Christian de Duve. A peroxisome is a membrane-bound organelle, a type of microbody, found in the cytoplasm of virtually all eukaryotic cells.
Who is credited with discovering Uncertainty principle?
Uncertainty principle: Werner Heisenberg. The uncertainty principle, also known as Heisenberg's indeterminacy principle, is a fundamental concept in quantum mechanics.
Who is credited with discovering Mensa?
Mensa (constellation): Nicolas Louis de Lacaille. Its name is Latin for table, though it originally commemorated Table Mountain and was known as "Mons Mensae".

Produced by the zona glomerulosa of the adrenal cortex, this mineralocorticoid is the body's key sodium-saver, quietly governing blood pressure and potassium balance in the kidney — which hormone is it?
Aldosterone is the main mineralocorticoid steroid hormone produced by the zona glomerulosa of the adrenal cortex in the adrenal gland.
This deep-tissue swelling — of the face, tongue, throat, or limbs — comes on within minutes to hours and is driven by either histamine or bradykinin — what is it?
Angioedema is an area of swelling (edema) of the lower layer of skin and tissue just under the skin or mucous membranes.
This general medical term describes a joint disorder in which the smooth cartilage lining wears away, leaving bone to grind directly on bone during movement — what condition is it?
Arthritis is a general medical term used to describe a disorder in which the smooth cartilagenous layer that lines a joint is lost, resulting in bone grinding on bone during joint movement.
Found in almost every habitat except the open sea and the poles, the order Coleoptera is the largest of all and accounts for about a quarter of every known animal species — which insects are these?
Beetle are insects that form the order Coleoptera, in the superorder Holometabola.
Born as Hughes Helicopters' Model 77 to replace the AH-1 Cobra, this twin-turboshaft attack helicopter packs a 30 mm chain gun and Hellfire missiles in a tandem cockpit — what is it?
Boeing AH-64 Apache (-) is an American twin-turboshaft attack helicopter with a tailwheel-type landing gear and a tandem cockpit for a crew of two.
This basic unit of digital information most often consists of eight bits, and is called an 'octet' in network protocol documents to avoid ambiguity. What is it?
Byte is a unit of digital information that most commonly consists of eight bits.
Portuguese explorers carried this tropical American tree to India in the 16th century; today Ivory Coast and India lead a 3.9-million-ton global harvest of its nut — what is it?
Cashew is the common name of a tropical evergreen tree Anacardium occidentale, in the family Anacardiaceae.
Born in 1847, this American wore three hats at once — psychologist, logician, and mathematician. Who was she?
Christine Ladd-Franklin (December 1, 1847 - March 5, 1930) was an American psychologist, logician, and mathematician.
This activity involves designing algorithms and writing code in high-level languages so a machine can follow step-by-step instructions to perform tasks. What is it?
Computer programming is the composition of sequences of instructions, called programs, that computers can follow to perform tasks.
This term describes all the material inside a cell's outer membrane, excluding the nucleus (in cells that have one) — its main components include a gel-like fluid called the cytosol. What is it?
Cytoplasm is all the material within a eukaryotic or prokaryotic cell, enclosed by the cell membrane, including the organelles and excluding the nucleus in eukaryotic cells.

Bred in the early twentieth century in Córdoba, Argentina, for hunting big game like wild boar and pumas, this large mastiff-type dog breed traces its ancestry partly to a now-extinct fighting dog — name the breed?
Dogo Argentino (plural Dogos Argentinos) is an Argentine breed of large dog of mastiff type.

This German chess champion — also a mathematician and philosopher — held the world title for 27 years, the longest reign ever, and was famed for a 'psychological' approach said to unsettle opponents. Who was he?
Emanuel Lasker (German; December 24, 1868 - January 11, 1941) was a German chess player, mathematician, and philosopher.
First confirmed around a pulsar in 1992, this astronomical term describes any planet located outside our own solar system — over 6,300 have now been confirmed — what is it called?
Exoplanet is a planet outside the Solar System. The first confirmed detection of an exoplanet was in 1992 around a pulsar, and the first detection around a main-sequence star was in 1995.
Sitting just below caesium as the second-most electropositive element, this alkali metal decays so fast that a bulk sample has never actually been seen — what is it?
Francium is a chemical element; it has symbol Fr and atomic number 87.

He shared a 1951 Nobel for synthesizing ten transuranium elements and developed the actinide concept that reshaped the periodic table; this American chemist later advised ten US presidents on nuclear policy — who was he?

Glenn T. Seaborg (April 19, 1912 - February 25, 1999) was an American chemist whose involvement in the synthesis, discovery and investigation of ten transuranium elements earned him a share of the 1951 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
Caused by a group of enteroviruses, this common infection opens with a fever and then sprinkles blistering spots on exactly the three body parts named in its label. What is it?
Hand, foot, and mouth disease (HFMD) is a common infection caused by a group of enteroviruses. It typically begins with a fever and feeling generally unwell.
This small rodent, with a pointed snout and a long, nearly hairless tail, has thrived by living alongside humans to the point that truly wild populations are now rare — what animal is it?
House mouse (Mus musculus) is a small mammal of the rodent family Muridae, characteristically having a pointed snout, large rounded ears, and a long and almost hairless tail.
This post-transition metal, chemically similar to gallium and thallium, was identified spectroscopically in 1863 and takes its name from the indigo line in its spectrum — what element is it?
Indium is a chemical element; its symbol is In and its atomic number is 49.
Director of Columbia's Center for Sustainable Development, which economist led the United Nations Millennium Project's work on the Millennium Development Goals?
Jeffrey Sachs (SAKS; born November 5, 1954) is an American economist and public policy analyst.
The world's longest venomous snake with an average length of 3.18 to 4 meters, endemic to Asia and widely distributed though not commonly encountered. What is it?
King cobra (Ophiophagus hannah) is a species complex of snakes endemic to Asia.
This German-born American businessman founded the first company to manufacture blue jeans, launching his San Francisco firm in 1853 — who is he?
Levi Strauss (STROWSS; born Lb Strau,; February 26, 1829 - September 26, 1902) was a German-born American businessman who founded the first company to manufacture blue jeans.
Over a 55-year career this American botanist bred more than 800 plant varieties, from the Shasta daisy to the Santa Rosa plum and a spineless cactus for cattle — who was he?

Luther Burbank (March 7, 1849 - April 11, 1926) was an American botanist, horticulturist, and pioneer in agricultural science who developed more than 800 strains and varieties of plants over his 55-year career.
In hermaphroditic species this reproductive pairing isn't strictly required, since self-fertilization is possible — what is the general term for it?
Mating refers to the pairing of either opposite-sex or hermaphroditic organisms for the purpose of sexual reproduction.
First flown by the Soviet Air Force in 1968 and still in Russian production today, this medium chopper carries the NATO reporting name 'Hip' — what aircraft is it?
Mil Mi-8 is a family of medium twin-turbine helicopters, originally designed by the Soviet Central Aerohydrodynamic Institute (TsAGI) in the 1960s and introduced into the Soviet Air Force in 1968.

Caused when fly larvae burrow into and feed on an animal's tissue, this parasitic infestation is triggered by open wounds but can occur on unbroken skin when species such as the botfly are involved — name this condition?
Myiasis (my-), also known as flystrike or fly strike, is the parasitic infestation of the body of a live animal by fly larvae (maggots) that grow inside the host while feeding on its tissue.
This American nuclear-capable subsonic stealth bomber, solely operated by the US Air Force, is designed as a flying wing to penetrate sophisticated air defenses. What is this aircraft?
Northrop B-2 Spirit is an American nuclear-capable subsonic stealth strategic bomber, often referred to as a "stealth bomber", solely operated by the United States Air Force.
Atomic number 8 and a potent oxidizing agent, this element pairs up into a colorless, odorless diatomic gas and tops the list of elements in Earth's crust — what is it?
Oxygen is a chemical element; it has the symbol O and its atomic number is 8.
This serous membrane lines the abdominal cavity, wrapping most internal organs in a single sheet of mesothelium that also carries their blood vessels and nerves — what's the membrane?
Peritoneum is the serous membrane forming the lining of the abdominal cavity or coelom in amniotes and some invertebrates, such as annelids.
Used in randomized clinical trials to gauge a treatment's true efficacy, this inert pill, injection, or sham surgery has no pharmaceutical effect of its own — what is it?
Placebo (pluh-) is a medicine or treatment intended to appear genuine to its recipient, but which has no pharmaceutical effect.

This endogenous steroid sex hormone plays a central role in the menstrual cycle, pregnancy, and embryonic development, and also serves as a key metabolic intermediate for producing other steroid hormones — name the hormone?
Progesterone (P4) is an endogenous steroid and progestogen sex hormone involved in the menstrual cycle, pregnancy, and embryogenesis of humans and other species.
Bitter-tasting and rich in vitamin K, this Mediterranean vegetable with edible buds resembling broccoli is also known as broccoli rabe — what is it?
Rapini (broccoli rabe or raab; RAHB) is a green cruciferous vegetable, with the leaves, buds, and stems all being edible; the buds somewhat resemble broccoli.
Discovered in 1973 by Ruth Bishop via electron micrographs, this virus is the leading cause of diarrheal disease in infants worldwide, spread via the fecal-oral route — what is it?
Rotavirus are the most common cause of diarrhoeal disease among infants and young children.
Central nervous system depressants in this drug class are often grouped with hypnotics, though technically they're meant to calm rather than induce sleep — what class of drug is this?
Sedative is a substance that induces sedation by reducing irritability or excitement.
With symbol Na from the Neo-Latin 'natrium' and a single stable isotope, this reactive metal sits in group 1 and is found in minerals like halite and feldspar — what is it?
Sodium is a chemical element; it has symbol Na (from Neo-Latin natrium) and atomic number 11.

This eye disorder causes the eyes to misalign when looking at an object; if it develops in childhood it often leads to a 'lazy eye,' while adult onset usually causes double vision instead — what condition is it?
Strabismus is an eye disorder in which the eyes do not properly align with each other when looking at an object.
Named for a U.S. state where its discovery research was based, this synthetic element (symbol Ts) holds the second-highest atomic number of all and was the most recently discovered — what is it?
Tennessine is a synthetic element; it has symbol Ts and atomic number 117.
These brightly colored Neotropical birds are known for their oversized, vividly patterned bills, and their chicks hatch completely naked with no down feathers at all — what bird is it?
Toucan are Neotropical birds in the family Ramphastidae.
This member of the herpesvirus family causes chickenpox in children and, upon reactivation later in life, shingles in adults — what is it called?
Varicella zoster virus (VZV), also known as human herpesvirus 3 (HHV-3, HHV3), is one of nine known herpes viruses that can infect humans.
Neither an insect nor a parasite despite its common name, this terrestrial crustacean is one of the few of its kind to have colonized dry land, likely since the late Paleozoic — what is it?
Woodlouse are terrestrial isopods in the suborder Oniscidea.
Formed when acetic acid combines with a base, this ion is also nature's most common building block for biosynthesis — what is it?
Acetate: Salt formed from acetic acid and a base.
Also known as thymol seeds, bishop's weed, or carom, this Apiaceae herb's fruit is often mistaken for lovage seed — what is it?
Nicknamed the death cap, this deadly poisonous fungus resembles edible species like Caesar's mushroom and is native to Europe — what is it?
Amanita phalloides: Poisonous mushroom (death cap). The large fruiting bodies appear in summer and autumn; the caps are generally greenish in colour with a white stipe and gills.
Native to the eastern Mediterranean, this flowering herb's seeds taste similar to fennel, licorice, and tarragon and flavor candies and spirits — what is it?
The clinging seed burrs of this plant genus, commonly known as burdock, directly inspired the invention of the hook-and-loop fastener — which genus?
This British mathematician and logician coined the phrase 'mathematical induction' and gave his name to a pair of laws relating conjunction, disjunction, and negation. Who was he?
Augustus De Morgan: British mathematician and logician (1806–1871)

This single-engine turboprop trainer, a license-built version of the Swiss Pilatus PC-9, replaced America's Cessna 'Tweet' and Turbo Mentor trainers in the 2010s and flies under the nickname 'Efroni' in Israel — which aircraft?
Beechcraft T-6 Texan II: Single-engine, low-wing tandem-seat turboprop military training aircraft.
This flowering vine's dried fruit is one of the most commonly traded spices in the world, its heat coming from a compound called piperine — what plant?
Black pepper: Ground fruit of the family Piperaceae.

Commonly known as mad cow disease, this fatal neurodegenerative illness in cattle is caused by a misfolded prion and can spread to humans as a variant of Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease. What is this cattle disease called?
Bovine spongiform encephalopathy: Fatal neurodegenerative disease of cattle. The United Kingdom was afflicted with an outbreak of BSE and vCJD in the 1980s and 1990s.
Designed in 1959 and partly based on Grace Hopper's FLOW-MATIC, this English-like programming language still runs mainframe banking systems today — what is it?
COBOL: Programming language with English-like syntax.
This involuntary, striated tissue forms the thick middle layer of the heart wall, with individual cells joined by structures called intercalated discs — what is it?
Cardiac muscle: Muscular tissue of heart in vertebrates.

Making up the brain's outer layer of neural tissue, this six-layered structure handles attention, memory, language, and consciousness, and is folded to fit more surface area inside the skull — what is it called?
Cerebral cortex: Outer layer of the cerebrum of the mammalian brain.

An essential nutrient your liver can only partly produce on its own, this compound builds phospholipids in cell membranes and helps make a neurotransmitter for muscle control, and occurs naturally in eggs, meat, and fish — which nutrient?
Choline: Chemical compound and essential nutrient. Choline is a cation with the chemical formula [(CH3)3NCH2CH2OH]+.

This ancient insect order traces back to the Late Jurassic, with chewing-mouthpart ancestors called "roachoids" scuttling around some 320 million years ago — yet only about 30 of its 4,600 species ever moved in with us. Which creature is it?
Cockroach: Insects of the order Blattodea.
Thanks to a variation in the gene OR6A2, some people taste this herb — called cilantro in the US — as fresh and citrusy while others swear it tastes like soap. What is it?
Coriander: Annual herb. Coriander, or Coriandrum sativum, is an annual herb in the family Apiaceae.
Once sold under the brand name Flexeril and chemically similar to tricyclic antidepressants, this oral medication treats sudden muscle spasms — what's the drug?
Cyclobenzaprine: Muscle relaxant medication. It should not be used together with MAOIs.
Caused by about 40 types of fungus and often picked up in public showers or contact sports like wrestling, this infection produces a red, itchy, scaly circular rash — what is it?
Dermatophytosis: Fungus infection of the skin. Dermatophytosis, also known as tinea and ringworm, is a fungal infection of the skin (a dermatomycosis), that may affect skin, hair, and nails.

Originally developed to compete for a USAF aerial-tanker contract it lost to Boeing's Stratotanker, this four-engined jetliner instead entered airline service with Delta in 1959 — what aircraft was it?
Douglas DC-8: American four-engined jet airliner family.

Carried out mainly at power plants, this process transforms heat from burning fuel or nuclear fission — or the motion of water and wind — into power used by homes and businesses. What is this process called?
Electricity generation: Process of generating electrical power.
He coined the term 'quantum entanglement' in 1935 and shared the 1933 Nobel Prize in Physics with Paul Dirac for his work on atomic theory — who is he?

Native to a huge swath of Eurasia but declared a noxious species in New South Wales after damaging native fish, this predatory freshwater game fish is known locally in Australia as 'redfin' — which fish?

These small to medium passerine birds have stout conical bills for cracking seeds and nuts, a worldwide native range excluding Australia and the poles, and include canaries, siskins, and Darwin's famous Galápagos group — what bird family is this?
Finch: Family of birds. The true finches are small to medium-sized passerine birds in the family Fringillidae.

This German chemist won a Nobel Prize for inventing a process that synthesizes ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen gas — a breakthrough that today supports nearly half the world's food production. Who is he?
Also known as cranesbills for their pointed seed pods, this 422-species genus bears five-petaled, often veined flowers and includes at least one protocarnivorous species — what's the genus?
This system of rules governing clauses, phrases, and word use is often absorbed unconsciously in childhood, long before anyone studies its syntax formally — what field?
Grammar: Structural rules of a language.

Marketed under a well-known brand name, this typical antipsychotic treats everything from schizophrenia to Tourette tics, but carries risks of tardive dyskinesia and dangerous QT-interval prolongation — what drug is it?
Haloperidol: Typical antipsychotic medication. Haloperidol, sold under the brand name Haldol among others, is a typical antipsychotic medication.
Some called egrets and others bitterns, these 75 species of long-legged, long-beaked wading birds make up the family Ardeidae — what are they?
Heron: Family of birds. The OED also observes that shiterow or shederow are terms used for herons, and also applied as derogatory terms meaning a thin, weakly person.
A colorless, flammable liquid with an ammonia-like odor, this N2H4 compound foams polymer plastics, fills airbag gas generators, and serves as a storable spacecraft propellant. What is it?
Hydrazine: Colorless flammable liquid with an ammonia-like odor. It is a simple pnictogen hydride, and is a colourless flammable liquid with an ammonia-like odour.
Designed in 1967 to replace the An-12 and haul heavy machinery into remote, poorly served regions, this four-engine Soviet airlifter earned the NATO name 'Candid' — what is it?
Ilyushin Il-76: Russian heavy four-engined military transport jet aircraft.
The biggest cat in the Americas, it has a bite so powerful it can crack a turtle's shell or punch straight through a skull between the ears — which animal?
Jaguar: Large cat native to the Americas.
Trained originally in mathematics at Cambridge, this English economist's Depression-era writings became the foundation for a whole school of macroeconomic thought bearing his name — who is he?
This classical physics model imagines matter as countless invisible particles in constant, random collisions, explaining pressure, temperature and viscosity alike — what is it?
Kinetic theory of gases: Understanding of gas properties in terms of molecular motion.
He fathered the Ford Mustang in the 1960s, then rescued Chrysler from collapse as its CEO in the 1980s — one of the rare executives to run two of Detroit's Big Three. Who?
Nicknamed for the Greek goddess of wisdom, this roughly 22-centimeter nocturnal bird was introduced to Britain in the late 1800s and to New Zealand's South Island soon after — which species?
Little owl: Species of owl. It was introduced into Britain at the end of the 19th century and into the South Island of New Zealand in the early 20th century.
Nicknamed the 'maker of modern Mysore,' this Indian civil engineer and statesman's birthday is now celebrated as Engineer's Day across India, Sri Lanka, and Tanzania — who is he?
M. Visvesvaraya: Indian civil engineer, administrator, and former prime minister of Mysore Kingdom.

Studying under Rutherford at the Cavendish Lab, this Adelaide-born physicist discovered the nuclei of helium-3 and tritium and helped achieve the first experimental nuclear fusion — who was this Australian humanitarian?
Long before chemists called it 3,4,5-trimethoxyphenethylamine, this psychedelic was drawn from peyote and San Pedro cacti for spiritual ceremonies — which naturally occurring compound is it?
Mescaline: Naturally occurring psychedelic compound. The practice of ingesting mescaline-containing cacti extracts dates back over 6,000 years.

The only woman among Einstein's classmates at Zurich Polytechnic, this Serbian mathematician was his first wife and is still debated as a possible collaborator on his 1905 miracle-year papers. Who was she?
Mileva Marić: Wife of Albert Einstein (1875–1948)
Grown above the upper lip and below the nose, this facial hair style has taken many forms across history — what is it called?
Moustache: Strip of facial hair across the upper lip. A moustache (UK:) or mustache (US:) is a growth of facial hair grown above the upper lip and under the nose of men.

Attributed to 19th-century pathologist Rudolf Virchow, this term for the premature death of cells caused by trauma or infection contrasts with the body's own programmed cell death — what's the condition called?
Necrosis: Unprogrammed cell death caused by external cell injury.
This carnivorous freshwater fish, found widely across cold waters worldwide, has a current all-tackle world record of 25 kg, caught in Germany in 1986 — what species is it?
Northern pike: Species of fish. The northern pike (Esox lucius), also known as jack, northern or simply pike, is a species of carnivorous fish of the genus Esox (pikes).
A woody perennial native to the Mediterranean and a close relative of sweet marjoram, this mint-family herb is a staple of Italian and Greek cooking — what is it?
This term describes the bulk functional tissue of an organ like the brain or lungs, the filler tissue inside flatworms, and certain leaf cross-section layers in plants — what is it?
Parenchyma: Visceral tissue found inside organs of animals.
In mathematics, what term describes both an ordered arrangement of a set's members and the act of rearranging them, as seen in the six possible orderings of three distinct numbers?
Permutation: Mathematical version of an order change.
Manufactured in Switzerland since 1991, this pressurized single-engine turboprop's large aft cargo door has made it popular with air-ambulance operators and police departments alike — which aircraft?
Pilatus PC-12: Swiss executive and utility transport aircraft.
Emerging in the 1960s as scholars from once-colonized nations began writing back, this academic field examines the lingering cultural and political effects of empire — what's it called?
Postcolonialism: Study of the cultural legacy of colonialism and imperialism.
This emotional response to severe distressing events like violence or a life-threatening injury can trigger flashbacks, panic attacks, insomnia, and post-traumatic stress disorder — what's it called?
Psychological trauma: Emotional response caused by severe distressing events.
This genus of roughly 1,750 flowering plant species includes the buttercups, spearworts, and water crowfoots — which genus?
Ranunculus: Genus of flowering plants in the buttercup family.
Its seeds yield castor oil but also harbor a highly potent toxin — which plant genus, better known for producing the castor bean?
Ricinus: Monotypic genus of plant in the spurge family.
Belonging to the order Urodela and reaching their greatest diversity in the Appalachian Mountains, these tailed, lizard-shaped amphibians never have more than four front toes — what are they?
Salamander: Order of amphibians. All ten extant salamander families are grouped together under the order Urodela, the sole surviving order from the group Caudata.
Co-founder of the file-sharing service Napster, this entrepreneur became Facebook's first president before later founding a philanthropic foundation focused on life sciences — who is he?
Sean Parker: American entrepreneur and philanthropist (born 1979)
Blurring the line between a single creature and a colony, this cnidarian is actually made of specialized zooids from one fertilized egg working together to float, feed and jet-propel — what is it?
Siphonophore: Order of colonial hydrozoans with differentiated zooids.
This family of roughly 1,450 moths flies so swiftly on narrow wings and streamlined bodies that some species hover at flowers and are routinely mistaken for hummingbirds — what's its scientific name?
Sphingidae: Family of insects. The Sphingidae are a family of moths commonly called sphinx moths, also colloquially known as hawk moths, with many of their caterpillars known as hornworms.

Distinct from addiction, this biopsychological condition occurs when a person's body has adapted so much to a psychoactive drug that stopping triggers withdrawal, requiring continued use just to function — what is this condition called?
Substance dependence: Need for a drug, whose discontinuation results in withdrawal symptoms.
This genus of flowering plants, commonly called dandelions, thrives nearly worldwide in yards, gardens, and roadsides — which genus?
Taraxacum: Genus of flowering plants in the family Asteraceae.
This French aerospace engineer flew to the International Space Station twice, first as a 2016 European Space Agency flight engineer and again in 2021 aboard a SpaceX Crew Dragon — who is he?
Thomas Pesquet: French aerospace engineer, pilot, and astronaut.
Commonly nicknamed a "mini-stroke," this brief disruption of blood flow to the brain causes stroke-like symptoms that fully resolve within 24 hours — what medical event is it?
Transient ischemic attack: Minor form of stroke.
This group of large hoofed mammals splits into odd-toed members like horses and rhinos, and even-toed members like cattle, giraffes, and camels — what are they called?
Ungulate: Group of mammals that walk on the tips of their toes or hooves.
Running a boutique called Sex with partner Malcolm McLaren, this English designer helped bring punk fashion into the mainstream and shaped the look of the Sex Pistols — who is she?
A short-legged, stubby-tailed marsupial native to Australia, this burrowing animal can weigh up to 35 kilograms and survives in an isolated pocket of central Queensland — which creature?
Wombat: Species of marsupial native to Australia.
Protactinium is denoted by which symbol?
The symbol for protactinium is Pa. Protactinium is a chemical element; it has symbol Pa and atomic number 91.
The symbol for polonium is Po. Polonium is a chemical element; it has symbol Po and atomic number 84.

Sebastian Maniscalco is a comedian. Sebastian Maniscalco (Italian: [maniˈskalko]; born July 8, 1973) is an American stand-up comedian and actor.

In what year was Rachel McAdams born?
Rachel McAdams: Rachel Anne McAdams (born November 17, 1978) is a Canadian actress.
In what year was Natasha Richardson born?
Natasha Richardson: Natasha Jane Richardson (11 May 1963 – 18 March 2009) was an English actress.

Hrithik Roshan: Roshan has frequently collaborated with his father, Rakesh Roshan.
In what year was Paul Rudd born?
Paul Rudd: Paul Stephen Rudd (born April 6, 1969) is an American actor.
In what year was Idris Elba born?
Idris Elba: Sir Idrissa Akuna Elba ( IH-driss; born 6 September 1972) is an English actor, DJ, rapper, and producer.
In what year was Jodie Foster born?
Jodie Foster: Alicia Christian "Jodie" Foster (born November 19, 1962) is an American actress and filmmaker.
In what year was Gillian Anderson born?
